Series::max_pair¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

std::pair<Series, Series> Series::max_pair(
    std::int64_t dim,
    bool keepdim = false) const

Why This Method Exists¶

max_pair() answers two inseparable questions about every lane of an axis: what is its largest value, and which source position supplied that value? It returns those answers together so the value and its provenance cannot drift apart through a second, independently written reduction.

The first member of the pair contains values. The second contains local int64 indices measured along dim. For a rank-2 input reduced across columns, for example, each index is a column number within its row; it is not a flat offset into storage.

Use max_pair() when later work needs both channels, such as retaining the winning score while gathering an aligned label from the same position. Use max() when only values matter, and argmax() when only positions matter.

Parameters¶

Parameter

Meaning

Default

dim

Axis whose lanes compete. Negative axes count backward from the final axis.

Required

keepdim

Keep the reduced axis with extent 1 in both returned Series.

false

dim names exactly one axis; there is no whole-Series overload. For rank-2 shape [R, C], reducing dim=0 returns one winner per column, while reducing dim=1 or dim=-1 returns one winner per row.

Return Contract¶

The return value is std::pair<Series, Series>:

Member

Dtype

Shape

Meaning

.first

Source dtype

Source shape with dim removed, or retained as 1

Winning values

.second

int64

Exactly the same shape as .first

Each winner’s local source index along dim

Both members stay on the source platform. The source is not mutated. A scalar source accepts dim=0 or dim=-1 and returns scalar value self paired with scalar index 0.

Ties, NaN, And Reverse Mode¶

If several positions contain the same maximum, the pair selects the first position along the reduced axis. The value and index are produced from that same selection, so they always describe one another.

That provenance also defines reverse mode. The value member is differentiable, and its incoming sensitivity is scattered back only to the reported index. The integer index member is discrete and does not carry sensitivity. This is a meaningful distinction from value-only max(dim): that reduction has no index to privilege and shares sensitivity across equal winners, whereas max_pair(dim).first follows the one winner named by .second.

NaN participates in the ordered-extremum kernel rather than being silently discarded. When NaN wins a lane, the paired index identifies the selected NaN position. Use a NaN-specific reduction when omission is the intended policy.

Execution Model¶

The CPU kernel scans each lane once and writes the winning value and its index together, matching the two-output reduction model. Reverse mode reuses that index as its scatter route rather than searching for the winner again. Returned Series own their result buffers; neither is a view of the receiver.

Examples¶

Example 1. Structured binding gives names to the value and provenance channels.

auto scores = pluss::make_series({
    {1.0, 7.0, 3.0},
    {4.0, 7.0, 6.0},
});

const auto [values, indices] = scores.max_pair(1);
std::cout << "values=" << values << "\n";
std::cout << "indices=" << indices;

Output¶

values=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[7, 7]
indices=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 1]

Each row contributes one winner. The indices are column positions, so both rows report 1 even though they occupy different flat storage ranges.

Example 2. A negative axis is normalized before reduction, and keepdim=true retains that axis in both members for later broadcasting.

const auto kept = scores.max_pair(-1, true);
std::cout << "values=" << kept.first << "\n";
std::cout << "indices=" << kept.second;

Output¶

values=pluss::Series(shape=[2,1], strides=[1,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[[7],
  [7]]
indices=pluss::Series(shape=[2,1], strides=[1,1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[[1],
  [1]]

Example 3. Ties choose the first position, and reverse mode follows precisely the index that the pair reports.

auto tied = pluss::make_series({
    {5.0, 5.0, 1.0},
    {2.0, 4.0, 4.0},
});
tied.tracks_slope_(true);

const auto result = tied.max_pair(1);
result.first.sum().reverse();

std::cout << "values=" << result.first << "\n";
std::cout << "indices=" << result.second << "\n";
std::cout << "dx=" << tied.sensitivity();

Output¶

values=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[5, 4]
indices=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 1]
dx=pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 0, 0],
  [0, 1, 0]]

The second equal maximum in each row receives zero sensitivity because it is not the position named by the paired index.

Example 4. A scalar still has one valid reduction position.

const auto result = pluss::make_series(42.0).max_pair(0);
std::cout << "value=" << result.first << "\n";
std::cout << "index=" << result.second;

Output¶

value=pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=42
index=pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=0

Example 5. A lane with no candidates cannot produce either a value or an index, so reduction over an empty axis fails before allocating a result.

try {
  std::cout << pluss::series::zeros({2, 0}).max_pair(1).first;
} catch (const std::exception& error) {
  std::string message = error.what();
  std::cout << message.substr(0, message.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

max_pair: cannot reduce an empty dimension

An undefined receiver, an out-of-range axis, complex ordered input, and an empty reduced axis are rejected. Empty non-reduced axes are valid because they contain no lanes requiring a winner.
